newsitem.title: ISRAEL: PLO, Israel wait for Albright decision.
newsitem.headline: PLO, Israel wait for Albright decision.

text.p: All sides to the Middle East peacemaking crisis had their eyes on Washington on Thursday, a day after U.S. envoy Dennis Ross ended a mission to revive Israel-PLO security cooperation.
"The ball is now in the Americans' court," Palestinian Authority cabinet secretary Ahmed Abdel-Rahman told Reuters.
U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright has said she would make her maiden visit to the troubled region at month's end if progress was made on the security front.
She said it was essential that Palestinian President Yasser Arafat make a "100 percent effort" to prevent militant attacks.
Her trip most likely would focus on reviving substantive negotiations frozen since Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu broke ground on a Jewish settlement in Arab East Jerusalem in March.
The Israeli army said it had lifted its siege, or ''internal closure'', of Hebron and Ramallah but the town of Bethlehem and an area surrounding Jerusalem remained sealed off.
The general ban against Palestinians from the West Bank and the Gaza Strip entering Israel remained in place.
Ross said before leaving on Wednesday his success in getting Israeli, Palestinian and U.S. security officials talking was a start in restoring security links.
Abdel-Rahman said he considered the resumption of trilateral security coordination a success but added:

"The American envoy must return to Washington convinced that what Netanyahu's government is demanding goes far beyond the security coordination and that this government is using the terrorist operation to destroy the whole peace process."
Ross's mission was spurred by a July 30 double suicide bombing on a Jewish market in Jerusalem that killed 16 people, including the attackers.

Israeli officials were not immediately available to comment on Ross's mission but Israel Radio said they worried Washington, despite Albright's saying she was waiting for results on the security front, already had a plan in hand to impose a solution on the sides regarding the wider crisis in peacemaking.
Israeli newspaper editorials and commentary were gloomy on the state of Middle East peacemaking.

Political analyst Shlomo Gazit wrote that the historic 1993 framework for Israel-PLO peacemaking reached in Oslo was dead and the sooner the sides acknowleged that the sooner they could begin framing a new way of making a final peace.
"The Oslo agreement is dead," Gazit wrote in the Maariv daily newspaper, saying the core trust that was Oslo's lifeblood was gone.

"The interest of both sides is to find a doctor that will recognise and declare (its) clinical death...that is the condition that will bring the sides' leaders to search for alternative ways and new political strategies."

Israel's mass circulation daily Yedioth Ahronoth said in an editorial on Netanyahu's talks with Jordan's King Hussein on Wednesday that on the bilateral level the sides should have been happy but were not: "Because on the bottom line the peace process is stuck."
King Hussein, trying to mediate between Israel and the Palestinians, failed to convince Netanyahu to lift sanctions imposed on Palestinians after the suicide attack.
Israel suspended peace talks and sealed off the two million Palestinians of the West Bank and Gaza Strip after the bombing. It halted financial transfers it owes the Authority.
Palestinians call Israel's measures collective punishment and demand they be lifted. Netanyahu insists they will remain in place until he has proof Arafat is cracking down on militants.
Arafat says he has fought militants. Abdel-Rahman said what Israel was after now was "security dictation" which violated Palestinian self-rule.
Israel has steadily lifted restrictions on Palestinian movements between towns in the West Bank but has insisted the main sanctions will remain firmly in place until Arafat acts.
Palestinians in Hebron said on Thursday that a 14-year-old boy seriously wounded in clashes with Israeli troops last month died in hospital.
